deep.reconstruction:
The page has no text, only coloured drawings on the back of a 1982 computer listing. The ideas below are a hedged reading of the pictures.

(1) Large figure (left): a planar cellular map drawn in blue. It has blue vertices (dots), long curved arcs that look like pieces of pseudo-lines, and a distinguished central vertex of degree about 7.
- Six or seven dark squares sit on the midpoints of the blue edges at that central vertex. Checking positions confirms this: each square lies on a radial blue edge.
- Green dots and edges sit inside the faces, so green looks like the dual graph or the face barycentres.
- Orange segments join edge-midpoints to face centres and vertices.
- The figure therefore looks like the barycentric (flag) subdivision of the map: vertices, edge-midpoints and face-centres, with the triangles built from them. Grothendieck uses exactly this vertex/edge/face coding for 'cartes' and dessins d'enfants.
- The squares and orange ring around the central vertex mark its closed star in that subdivision: a polygon whose corners alternate between edge-midpoints and face-centres.
- A grey pencil-hatched sector marks one corner, i.e. one flag or angle at the vertex.

(2) Top right: a blue star with eight half-edges. This is a single vertex where four lines (or pseudo-lines) cross, or equivalently a degree-8 vertex of a map.

(3) Bottom left: a blue star with a small orange circle, hatched, around the centre. Green dots mark where the circle meets the edges. This is a small disk neighbourhood of a vertex whose boundary circle is cut by the incident edges, i.e. the 'link' of the vertex.

(4) Bottom right: a blue vertex with about 8 rays, surrounded by a green polygon (the dual face or link) with orange triangles at some corners.
- A dashed blue line joins the centre to one triangle.
- This probably shows the local structure of the dual or barycentric subdivision around one vertex.
- It could also show a local modification: replacing a multiple crossing of pseudo-lines by small triangles, i.e. perturbing it into a simple arrangement.

(5) Bottom middle: a green dashed skeleton crossed by a black segment, with faint pencil rays. This is probably an edge and its dual edge, or a local cell picture.

In the context of cote 154 (systems of pseudo-lines), these are working sketches of the combinatorial cell decomposition of arrangements: maps, their duals and barycentric subdivisions, and the local picture at a multiple point. Nothing here is a stated result.
errors: No mathematical claims are made, so there is nothing to check; the reading of the colour coding is conjectural.

ideas.what: Barycentric/flag subdivision of a planar map, colour-coded by vertices, edge-midpoints and face-centres
ideas.modern_name: Flag (barycentric) subdivision of a map; cartographic group / dessin triangulation
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Tutte, Jones–Singerman 1978); Grothendieck for dessins d'enfants
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984), section on 'cartes' and cartographic groups

ideas.what: Local star/link of a multiple vertex (crossing point of several pseudo-lines), drawn as an 8-ray star and a small disk neighbourhood
ideas.modern_name: Link of a vertex / local structure of a multiple point in a pseudo-line arrangement

ideas.what: Possible resolution of a multiple point into small triangles (simple arrangement)
ideas.modern_name: Perturbation / simplification of an arrangement; triangle flips

deep.surprise_reason: These are textless sketches of standard combinatorial constructions: map, dual and barycentric subdivision, and the local star of a multiple point. They fit the pseudo-line and 'cartes' material of the period and contain no identifiable new result.
transcription_corrections: Dark squares in the large figure lie on the midpoints of the blue edges at the central vertex. They are not arbitrary marks: they are the edge-vertices of the barycentric subdivision.
The listing on the back is part of the same 19 Aug 82 JES2 job log as page 127; the transcription's '55 SYSOUT PRINT RECORDS' is probably the mirror image of '99' as given on page 127.
